articles.title: University of Tokyo Researchers Develop High-Speed Microscopy Technique
articles.summary: The University of Tokyo team has developed a high-speed microscopy technique that captures images nearly 400 times faster than previous methods.
articles.content: Researchers at the University of Tokyo have made significant strides in high-speed microscopy by developing a technique that captures images nearly 400 times faster than previous methods. This breakthrough enables scientists to create detailed "videos of living cells' dynamic processes. The team's innovative approach involves shining mid-infrared light on samples, which triggers a photothermal signal. By capturing snapshots of the resulting temperature-change signatures from different molecules within the cell, researchers can gather valuable information about cellular activity. This new technique has been shown to outperform previous high-speed microscopy methods by a significant margin. While earlier attempts at similar imaging captured only 0.05 images per second, the University of Tokyo team achieved an impressive rate of 19.2 images per second. By capturing multiple snapshots from various angles, researchers can build three-dimensional videos" that provide a more comprehensive understanding of active biological processes within living cells. This technique holds great promise for advancing our knowledge of cellular behavior and its response to treatments. The internal composition of a cell can be mapped by analyzing its unique frequency signatures. These signatures are then used to illuminate the cell with visible light, allowing researchers to visualize its internal structure. A key advantage of this technique is that it doesn't rely on dyes, which can be toxic to live cells and compromise experimental results. By combining images from multiple angles, a three-dimensional picture of the cell's internal composition can be created. The team behind this research has also developed a new method for capturing images at incredibly fast speeds. The team has successfully utilized their innovative microscopy technique to capture 3D images of living cells at unprecedented speeds. This achievement allows for a more detailed examination of cellular processes that were previously difficult to observe. Researchers can now use this method to track the movement and behavior of lipid droplets within cells, shedding light on how they regulate energy and store lipids. The MIP-ODT technique has been transformed from a static observation tool into a dynamic investigational instrument capable of quantifying rapid biological processes in three dimensions. One potential application for this breakthrough lies in studying biomolecular condensates, which are membraneless structures within cells containing proteins and nucleic acids. Abnormal behavior of these condensates has been linked to neurodegenerative disorders, making their study crucial for developing new treatments. The team aims to tackle fundamental biological questions that conventional techniques cannot answer. By providing quantitative information about the chemical composition of living cells, this label-free chemical imaging technique enables researchers to gain a deeper understanding of cellular dynamics and advance toward a more comprehensive measurement-driven comprehension of life. This innovative technique combines mid-infrared photothermal optical diffraction tomography with high-speed microscopy to capture 3D images of living cells at rates nearly 400 times faster than traditional methods. The resulting images provide a wealth of information about the chemical composition of individual cells, enabling researchers to gain a deeper understanding of cellular dynamics and ultimately advance toward developing more effective treatments for various diseases. Phys.org : https://phys.org/news/2026-10-high-microscopy-captures-3d-images.html

articles.title: Okinawa Institute of Science and Technology Researchers Study Enzyme Activity in Crowded Microenvironments
articles.summary: Researchers at the Okinawa Institute of Science and Technology have discovered that increased crowding can boost enzymatic activity in model protein-rich droplets. This phenomenon has significant implications for our understanding of cellular metabolism.
articles.content: Cells are teeming with activity as reactions unfold to sustain life. Within these microscopic environments, proteins and other molecules cluster together in membraneless compartments, creating distinct pockets for metabolic processes. These crowded microenvironments have a profound impact on enzyme function, yet the relationship between physical properties and enzymatic activity remains poorly understood. Researchers at the Okinawa Institute of Science and Technology (OIST) set out to explore this complex interaction. In model protein-rich droplets, researchers studied how enzymes interact with their surroundings, revealing an unexpected boost in enzymatic activity due to increased crowding. This phenomenon has significant implications for our understanding of cellular metabolism. The findings suggest that as enzymes become more active, they can also influence the flow within these crowded environments, creating a dynamic feedback loop between enzyme function and physical properties. Further investigation into this intricate relationship may provide valuable insights into the intricacies of cellular processes. Researchers at the Okinawa Institute of Science and Technology (OIST) created tiny droplets containing a protein called BSA to study how crowding affects enzyme activity. The droplets had varying concentrations of BSA, ranging from dilute to heavily packed. The scientists then added enzymes - lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) in one set of experiments and alcohol dehydrogenase (ADH) in another - along with their substrates to the model droplets. This allowed them to observe how crowding impacted the enzymes' ability to catalyze reactions. At first, increasing the concentration of BSA boosted enzyme activity, which may seem counterintuitive given that crowding typically slows down chemical reactions by limiting movement and increasing liquid viscosity. However, this effect only lasted until very high levels of BSA were reached. As the environment became increasingly crowded with BSA, researchers at RIKEN used computer simulations to examine how the structure of the enzymes changed. They found that in a dilute environment, an enzyme's active site is typically open, allowing substrates to bind and react. In contrast, as the surrounding environment becomes crowded with BSA, the enzyme's active site closes, which could explain why enzyme activity eventually declines at high levels of crowding. The simulations conducted by Laurino's team revealed a surprising twist on how enzyme reactions are affected by crowding. When the enzyme's active site is closed, it requires less energy for the reaction to occur, allowing it to happen more readily. To investigate further, Laurino and her team examined the impact of enzyme activity on the fluid dynamics within protein droplets. Through fluorescent tracer experiments, they found that active enzymes increased mobility within these crowded environments, enabling both BSA proteins and nanoparticles to move more freely. In contrast, droplets containing inactive enzymes exhibited higher viscosity, with molecules moving at a slower pace. This difference in behavior suggests that enzyme activity plays a crucial role in determining the dynamics of protein droplets. Theoretical models proposed by MPI-DS researchers suggest that enzyme activity creates chemical gradients within these droplets, inducing tiny flows that facilitate molecular movement and mixing. This phenomenon highlights how enzymes can have physical effects on larger scales. Laurino's team plans to explore whether this two-way interaction between enzymes and their environment applies to multienzyme complexes as well. They also intend to conduct experiments in bacterial cells to verify the validity of their findings under more complex biological conditions. Researchers have found that enzyme reactions can accelerate when enzymes are crowded together, but this effect is short-lived as protein droplets become increasingly packed. However, when these droplets reach a certain density, the reaction rate actually slows down due to steric hindrance and crowding effects. To further verify their findings, experiments will be conducted in bacterial cells to test the validity of their results under more complex biological conditions, providing a deeper understanding of enzyme behavior in crowded environments. This research can have significant implications for various fields, including biotechnology and medicine. Phys.org : https://phys.org/news/2026-10-crowding-enzyme-reactions-protein-droplets.html

articles.title: Heat from Crematoria Used to Warm Homes and Public Facilities
articles.summary: A groundbreaking experiment is underway in the UK, where excess heat from crematoria is being harnessed to warm homes and public facilities.
articles.content: A groundbreaking experiment is underway in the UK, where excess heat from crematoria is being harnessed to warm homes and public facilities. This innovative approach has sparked controversy among some local officials, who question its practicality. Critics argue that capturing heat from cremations amounts to little more than warming radiators with a tube, as Redditch and Bromsgrove Councils' Guy Revans put it. Despite initial backlash, the project has won recognition for its eco-friendly credentials and is now being replicated in other parts of Europe. Redditch's crematorium has been utilizing waste heat since 2013 to warm the local swimming pool. The facility conducts around 1,200 cremations annually, generating a modest but usable amount of excess heat. This heat is typically captured as part of a process that removes vaporized mercury from dental fillings in the flue gases emitted by the gas-fired ovens. The process involves using a heat exchanger to capture the excess heat before venting the remaining gas into the atmosphere. In essence, this method captures heat by default, leaving the question of whether it makes sense to waste or utilize this resource. The captured heat is then channeled through an underground water loop to supply the swimming pool with warmth. The Redditch experiment has sparked debate about the potential for utilizing crematoria waste heat on a larger scale. While some view it as a viable means of reducing carbon intensity in funeral rites, others remain skeptical about its practicality and feasibility. The use of crematoria as a source of heat is being explored in various parts of the world, with some projects already underway. One such example is the recreation center in the UK that has partnered with a local crematorium to utilize excess heat from the cremation process. This heat is then used to warm the pool and surrounding areas. The system in place at the recreation center has proven to be effective, saving the council tens of thousands of pounds per year in fuel costs. The combination of waste heat from the crematorium with gas-fired boilers allows for a more efficient use of energy. This approach has also been implemented at other locations, including a school currently under construction in Aberdeen, Scotland. The Aberdeen school will receive approximately half of its total heat requirement from the city's crematorium, with a heat pump covering the remaining needs. The system is expected to be fully operational by February 2027. This project highlights the potential for crematoria to provide a significant source of renewable energy. In Finland, a new crematorium set to open in 2028 will be connected to the town's district heat network, supplying over 6,500 homes with hot water for heating. The new crematorium in Kangasala, Finland will be fully electric and partly powered by solar panels on its roof, highlighting the innovative approach to energy efficiency in heating homes. Timo Heikkilä, an expert working on the project, emphasizes that using this facility for heat generation is a significant development. Winter temperatures in Kangasala can remain below 0 degrees Celsius for weeks on end, making efficient heating systems crucial for residents. Finland's reliance on natural gas for heating has been decreasing due to concerns over climate change and Russia's invasion of Ukraine, which had previously provided affordable gas supplies. As a result, the country is seeking alternative sources of heat, including waste heat from various facilities. In the UK, crematoria have also started adopting eco-friendly practices, such as scheduling the firing of gas ovens to match funeral services and holding coffins for up to 72 hours to optimize energy usage. Implementing heat recovery technology at crematoria in the US is a more complex process than in other countries due to the rarity of district heat networks and the private ownership of most crematoria facilities. This means that the investment required for heat exchangers and pipework necessary to connect buildings is significantly higher, making it less feasible for businesses to adopt this technology. Matthews Environmental Solutions, a company specializing in environmental solutions, is closely monitoring the situation and exploring potential opportunities for implementing heat recovery systems at US crematoria when the economic conditions are favorable. The company's director of strategy, Paul Seyler, emphasizes that utilizing waste heat from cremation flue gases would be a significant resource-saving measure, but notes that there are currently no fully operational systems in place in the US. The energy performance of the building is now displayed on an LED screen in the reception area, providing visitors with a visual representation of the impact of the heat exchanger's operation. While gas is still used for some heating needs and cremations, the new system has saved an estimated 29 metric tons of greenhouse gas emissions annually, a significant reduction in environmental impact. Hannah Rumble, associate at the University of Bath's Centre for Death and Society, notes that recovering heat from cremations is one way to mitigate the devastating effects humans have had on the environment, highlighting the importance of finding innovative solutions. Using waste heat from crematoria has been hailed as a sensible approach by some, including independent humanist funeral and wedding celebrant Gaynor Doherty in the UK, who suggests that natural burials might be preferred by many eco-conscious individuals. The carbon intensity of cremation varies across facilities but can reach around 250 kilograms of carbon per gas-fired cremation, with recovering heat from the process offsetting some emissions while still leaving a significant amount unaccounted for. Decarbonizing heat production is a complex challenge, but every effort counts in this endeavor. The innovative use of crematoriums as heat sources for homes and swimming pools may also hold emotional significance for those involved. Some individuals may appreciate the idea that their loved ones' warmth is being shared with others after they pass away. In Finland, an all-electric crematorium in Kangasala operates continuously, producing less heat than a gas-fired equivalent but running 24/7 due to its efficiency in topping up retained heat within ceramic ovens using electricity. The facility connects to the local district heat network, making it possible for mourners to feel the warmth generated by their loved one's cremation upon returning home. The project has led Heikkilä to contemplate his own end-of-life choices, with him expressing a desire to be cremated and have his waste heat recycled. This ease of use is a welcome feature in an era where home entertainment systems are becoming increasingly complex. However, some tests have revealed a notable limitation in the TV's ability to capture subtle skin tones, often resulting in less variation than what is seen on RGB models. In addition to its technical prowess, the S95H has undergone a design overhaul, with a sleek new silver bezel that adds a touch of sophistication to any living room. The revised design may be more to some people's taste than others, but it is undeniable that the new bezel has generated significant interest among consumers. The S95H marks an important milestone in the evolution of OLED technology, but it faces stiff competition from newer RGB models and art TVs that are pushing the boundaries of what is possible with television displays. The Samsung S95H OLED TV has undergone some design changes that affect its connectivity options. Gone is the One Connect breakout box, which was previously included in the package but can now be bought separately if desired. This change means users must connect their external devices directly to the television, a setup that may seem more straightforward without the additional device. While this shift does make the S95H slightly thicker than its predecessor at 1.04 inches compared to 0.4 inches for the S95F, it has some advantages in terms of convenience. Without the One Connect box, there's one less device to set up and manage, which can simplify the overall viewing experience. The S95H features a more traditional array of ports on its right side, including four HDMI connections. These are supplemented by an Ethernet jack for wired internet connectivity, optical audio out for surround sound, two USB ports for playing files from external storage drives, and a headphone jack. The TV also supports the latest Wi-Fi 6E standard for faster speeds and improved compatibility. The S95H's design allows it to be mounted flush to a wall, much like its predecessor. However, I opted to use the included pedestal stand during testing, which attached easily to the back of the television. This stand provides a stable base for the TV while also allowing for some flexibility in terms of placement. The user interface on the S95H is powered by Tizen OS, an operating system that has its fans but can be confusing for those unfamiliar with it. While I have experience with Tizen and was able to navigate the setup process without issue, others may find it more challenging than models running other interfaces like Google TV. One aspect of the S95H's design that I particularly appreciate is its remote control. Uncluttered and easy to use, it provides access to essential functions like channel selection, mute, and volume control, along with a few app shortcuts for popular services like Netflix. The Samsung remote stands in contrast to some other models on the market, such as those from Hisense, which often feature an overwhelming number of buttons. In my experience, most users can get by with a more streamlined approach to remotes, focusing on essential functions and key app shortcuts. The color accuracy of the Samsung S95H OLED TV has been put to the test in rigorous real-world evaluation, revealing its capabilities compared to other flagship models. Measuring up against the competition, the S95H delivers excellent color quality across various scenes and content types, but falls short in specific instances. The market for high-end TVs is increasingly saturated with top-notch options, making it no longer a straightforward choice to opt for Samsung's latest flagship model. A particularly demanding test case was the movie Awake, which features numerous dark scenes that often challenge even the most advanced TVs. Despite some initial struggles, the S95H ultimately performed well in these scenes, although requiring adjustments to achieve optimal results. The AI Optimized picture mode proved instrumental in enhancing color and clarity in several key scenes from Awake, outshining its predecessor, the Samsung Micro RGB R95H, in certain instances. This feature not only improved overall image quality but also demonstrated the S95H's ability to showcase contrast and depth simultaneously. A similar success story unfolded with The Creator, where AI Optimized helped reveal a wealth of texture details in a dark scene featuring cliffs that would otherwise appear dull on some OLED and RGB TVs. This performance suggests that the S95H's OLED technology is capable of delivering high-quality visuals, including deep blacks, contrast, and clarity. The Samsung S95H OLED TV has proven itself to be a capable performer when it comes to color representation. A scene from The End of Oak Street showcased people wearing brightly colored shirts without any noticeable color blooming or bleeding. In contrast, the Super Mario Galaxy Movie is often used as a benchmark for color bloom testing, and the S95H exceeded expectations in this regard. Interestingly, the TV's Filmmaker picture mode, which can sometimes make movies appear too dark, actually corrected for color bloom issues in the Galaxy movie. The OLED technology in the S95H also excelled when rendering darker scenes with complex colors. A particularly challenging scene from Guardians of the Galaxy Vol 2 showcased a dark uniform with excellent shadow detail, demonstrating the TV's ability to handle nuanced color gradations. One notable aspect of OLED technology is its ability to render blacks and grays with exceptional depth and clarity by adjusting or turning off individual pixels as needed. This feature was evident in a scene from Game of Thrones where an army at night was depicted with good results when using AI Optimized mode, but would otherwise appear too dark. A skin tone test revealed some minor issues with the S95H's color accuracy, particularly in scenes featuring multiple people. In one instance, there wasn't enough variance in color between individuals to make them easily distinguishable from one another. The TV also exhibited some minor flaws when rendering certain nature scenes, such as a demo reel showcasing various outdoor environments. For example, grass appeared slightly less vibrant and detailed compared to the LG Micro RGB Evo in one scene near a fence, while dark trees in a forest scene still retained plenty of shadow detail. When viewing a benchmark demo, it's clear that OLED technology has an edge over RGB in rendering blacks and grays regardless of the content being displayed. OLED's color capabilities are also on par with those of RGB, as evidenced by a scene featuring a yellow flower and a red cactus that appeared brighter than any RGB model I've tested. In particular, a 4K Ultra playback of Blade Runner 2049 showcased yellows and reds in one scene that looked hyper-realistic, almost like you could reach out and peel the color off the screen. On other RGB models from Sony, Hisense, and even Samsung, colors were not as sharp or vibrant as those on the S95H OLED TV. Moving to gaming tests, I was impressed by the picture quality, refresh rate, and sound of the S95H. A library scene in Resident Evil Requiem lacked texture and detail compared to some RGB models and projectors I've tested. However, when playing Red Dead Redemption 2 at 165 Hz, the S95H looked crisp and felt responsive, especially during a lakeside horse ride scene that showcased incredible detail on the main character's face. In other gaming tests, such as playtesting Senua’s Saga: Hellblade II on an Xbox Series X with AI Optimized picture mode enabled, the main character's face appeared a bit dark. The anti-glare technology on the Samsung S95H OLED TV is effective in reducing glare, but it's not a standout feature compared to other TVs from the same brand. Viewing artwork on this model is a treat, thanks to its OLED display and anti-glare screen. However, accessing most paintings requires a $5 monthly subscription to the Samsung Art Store. It's worth noting that the Samsung The Frame Pro 2026 still offers better art viewing capabilities. The S95H is an exceptional TV with impressive picture quality features, including deep blacks, excellent contrast, accurate color, and AI Optimized mode. However, its performance in certain tests lags behind some of its competitors, particularly high-end RGB models like the LG Micro RGB Evo. Despite this, the Samsung S95H stands out as a top-tier television option in many real-world tests, albeit slightly less capable than some other options available in the market today. articles.title: Indonesia Suffered Estimated 3,560 Deaths Due to Wildfire Pollution in September
articles.summary: A new study has revealed that Indonesia suffered an estimated 3,560 deaths in September due to pollution from smoke emitted by wildfires across the country.
articles.content: A new study has revealed that Indonesia suffered an estimated 3,560 deaths in September due to pollution from smoke emitted by wildfires across the country. This alarming figure was made possible by months of devastating forest and land fires that blanketed the Southeast Asian archipelago with hazardous air. According to data released by the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA), a Helsinki-based think tank, approximately 57.8 million people in Indonesia were exposed to unhealthy to hazardous air conditions during this period. The CREA study estimated the number of deaths caused by short-term exposure to PM2.5 pollution, which are small particles that can penetrate deep into the lungs or bloodstream and have been linked to a higher risk for illness and premature death by the World Health Organization. This increase in deaths is not surprising given the severity of the air quality crisis in Indonesia during September 2026, with CREA highlighting a twofold rise from their August estimate. Most of the estimated deaths attributed to fire pollution in Indonesia occurred on Borneo island, particularly in the eastern part of the country, as well as on Java and Sumatra islands. The researchers also examined nonfire pollution from urban power generation, industry, and transportation, which contributed to an additional 1,750 deaths in September. This brings the total number of fatalities attributed to air pollution in the country to 5,310, out of a population of approximately 290 million people. According to the report, exposure levels to PM2.5 particles exceeded the World Health Organization's annual threshold by a significant margin in September. Nationally, the threshold was breached by over seven times, while in Sumatra it was exceeded tenfold, and an alarming twenty-four times in Kalimantan on Borneo. The severe air pollution has led to a surge in acute respiratory infections across the country, with more than 330,000 cases recorded nationwide. The devastating impact of Indonesia's wildfires continues to unfold, with experts attributing the majority of the blame to slash-and-burn land-clearing practices carried out by companies in the timber, palm oil, and mining sectors. On the island of Java, where Jakarta is located, a significant portion of air pollution-related deaths were not caused by the fires themselves. According to the CREA report, between 73% and 80% of these fatalities, totaling around 1,530 in September, can be linked to non-fire sources such as industrial activities, vehicle emissions, and waste burning. This stark reality highlights the danger posed by air pollution from sources other than wildfires. As one expert pointed out, these non-fire pollutants are just as hazardous as smoke from burning forests and peatlands. The government's preparedness for disaster management has been criticized for being woefully inadequate, with budget cuts hindering the efforts of the national disaster management agency. The CREA report has emphasized the need for Indonesia to transition from solely responding to wildfires to restoring peatlands that have been drained and made vulnerable to fires. This shift in approach must be accompanied by strict enforcement of laws against land clearing through burning, as well as increased accountability for companies operating on concession lands. This includes measures to prevent damage caused by their operations. The government has defended its efforts to combat the fires, citing the deployment of over 72,000 personnel in cloud-seeding and firefighting operations, activation of more than 2,100 medical professionals in affected areas, and distribution of 5.3 million masks. articles.title: Dark Eden by Chris Beckett Explored in New Scientist Book Club
articles.summary: The novel Dark Eden by Chris Beckett has been analyzed by the New Scientist Book Club as part of their journey through the book.
articles.content: The New Scientist Book Club has embarked on a journey through the novel Dark Eden by Chris Beckett. The story begins as the protagonist navigates a path that winds its way through a cluster of starflowers, their delicate petals shimmering in the fading light. As they emerge from the starflower thicket, the landscape opens up to reveal a clearing where a group of Batwing adults and newhairs are gathered around a giant redlantern tree. Armed with blackglass axes, they're working tirelessly to harvest the tree's flowers, which cast a warm pink glow over the scene. The protagonist and their companions make their way around the edge of the clearing, pushing aside branches at Family Fence and entering the open forest beyond. Gone are the shelters and campfires that had marked their previous journey; now, they're surrounded by towering trees that stretch up towards the sky like giant pillars. As they walk through the forest, the trees begin to make a strange noise - a low, rumbling hum that echoes through the landscape. The forest itself seems to be responding to their presence, its very fabric vibrating with an otherworldly energy. The air is filled with the sweet scent of blooming flowers and the distant calls of birds. Eventually, they come across Lava Blob, a large rock formation where they can rest and replenish their supplies. Old Roger hands out seedcakes made from ground-up starflower seeds, which provide a welcome sustenance for the weary travelers. As they settle in to rest, they're surrounded by the sounds of the forest, including the chirping calls of yellow animals called hoppers that bounce through the underbrush on their hind legs. The forest creatures that inhabited the underbrush seemed to be getting more and more annoying as the days passed. The hoppers, in particular, were a nuisance, their chirping calls piercing the air as they bounced through the underbrush on their hind legs. To deal with them, the group would often resort to throwing stones to scare them off. As the sun rose higher in the sky, the Starry Swirl continued to shine brightly overhead. The light cast long shadows across the forest floor, illuminating the various types of plants and trees that grew there. Redlanterns, whitelanterns, and spiketrees stood tall among the foliage, their leaves rustling softly in the breeze. The air was filled with a cacophony of sounds as the group made their way through the forest. Flutterbyes flitted about, their iridescent wings glimmering in the sunlight. Bats chased after them, adding to the commotion. The trees themselves seemed to hum a gentle tune, their branches swaying softly back and forth. After several hours of walking, the group came across a small pool filled with shiny wavyweed. The newhairs, eager for a break from their journey, quickly shed their wraps and dove into the warm water. They spent some time swimming and playing in the pool, snatching up crabfish and oysters to eat. As they rested by the pool, the boys couldn't help but admire Tina Spiketree's athleticism as she dove back into the water. Her long legs seemed to slice through the surface with ease, and her smooth skin glistened in the sunlight. It was clear that she had caught their attention, not just because of her physical prowess, but also due to her undeniable beauty. The group continued on their journey, eventually reaching the foot of the Peckham Hills, which rose up from the forest floor like giants. They began their ascent via a winding path known as the Monkey Path, a route that had been used by generations of Family members before them. The forest floor gave way to a winding path known as the Monkey Path, which had been used by generations of Family members before them. This route led through a sea of towering trees, their trunks thick and gnarled with age. Redlanterns, whitelanterns, and scalding hot spiketrees dominated the landscape, their branches swaying gently in the breeze. Below these towering sentinels, flickering starflowers bloomed, adding a touch of vibrancy to the forest floor. The air was cool and damp, filled with the scent of leaves and the distant tang of water. Streams ran through the forest, flowing down from the darkness and ice that lay beyond the treeline. As we made our way up the path, small creatures known as monkeys darted between the trees. These agile beings had slender bodies and six long arms, each ending in a delicate hand. They were quick and nimble, their movements seemingly effortless as they leapt from branch to branch. One of these monkeys met its end at the hands of Handsome Fox, who shot it with an arrow. While the creature was ultimately nothing more than bones and sinew, Fox was pleased with his marksmanship, if only because the monkey's swift movements made it a challenging target. As we continued our ascent, the forest began to change around us. The starflowers disappeared, replaced by smaller trees that seemed to shrink away from the light. The monkeys vanished too, leaving behind only an occasional smallbuck darting through the underbrush. Finally, the trees gave way to open ground, and we emerged onto the top edge of the forest. From this vantage point, the breathtaking vista unfolded before us. Circle Valley stretched out below, a vast expanse of lanterns shining like diamonds in the fading light. The landscape seemed endless, with the Blue Mountains looming darkly in the distance, their shadows cast across the valley floor. The vast expanse of the landscape stretched out before us, a seemingly endless sea of grasslands and rocky outcroppings. Above it all, the majestic spiral of Starry Swirl shone brightly in the sky. As we stood there, the darkness seemed to press in around us, making every step feel like a challenge. The lack of trees meant no warm glow from lanternflowers or gentle heat from trunks, leaving only the faint light from the star and the forest's edge to guide our way. The air was biting cold, especially on our bare feet, which were exposed to the elements. It was a cruel contrast to the warmth that would have been provided by trees, had they not been absent from this unforgiving landscape. Many of my companions hesitated at the prospect of running up the snowy hill, but I convinced Gerry, who was younger than me by only a wombtime, to join me on the dare. We bundled up in our waistwraps and buckskins, trying to ward off the chill. As we climbed higher, the cold began to seep into our bones, making every step feel like a struggle. "It's burning! Gerry exclaimed, his teeth chattering with the effort of speaking. The silence was oppressive, a heavy blanket of stillness that wrapped around us like a shroud. No signs of life could be heard anywhere - no rustling leaves, no chirping birds, no buzzing insects. The only sound was the gentle gurgling of water as it flowed from under the snow in countless tiny streams. The darkness was absolute, with not even the faint glow of tree lights to illuminate our surroundings. We were forced to rely on the soft luminescence of Starry Swirl to navigate our way through the desolate landscape. Even that light was weak and diffused, making it difficult for us to see each other's faces. I couldn't help but think about Earth, the place where Tommy and Angela first came from, with the Three Companions guiding them on their journey. It was a world vastly different from our own, with its own unique features and wonders. One of those wonders was a massive star that illuminated the planet with an intense, blinding light. As we stood there in the darkness, I mentioned Earth's giant star to Gerry, who responded with a shivering nod. His teeth were chattering uncontrollably, making it difficult for him to speak. The extract from Chris Beckett's novel Dark Eden" continues to delve into the protagonist's thoughts about the mysterious phenomenon known as Night. The author's use of simple yet poignant language effectively conveys the character's introspection and wonder. As the darkness looms, the protagonist reflects on its significance, recalling that it was indeed referred to as Night by others. This subtle detail adds depth to the narrative, hinting at a complex world with its own terminology and culture. The passage concludes with the protagonist's contemplative musings about the nature of this enigmatic force. articles.title: Life Thrives on Sunless Planet According to Science Fiction Novel
articles.summary: A science fiction novel has sparked a thought-provoking idea about life on a planet without sunlight, exploring the possibility of free-floating planets existing without suns and supporting life.
articles.content: A science fiction novel has sparked a thought-provoking idea about life on a planet without sunlight. Chris Beckett's Dark Eden tells the story of a world where life thrives in the absence of solar radiation. The author came up with this concept in 1992 for a short story called The Circle of Stones. At that time, Beckett was unaware that planets without suns do exist in our galaxy and beyond. However, he hypothesized that it's possible for life to emerge on such worlds. This idea is supported by the existence of thermal vents in Earth's deep ocean, which harbor unique ecosystems devoid of sunlight. Some scientists even believe that life on our planet may have originated in these dark environments. Beckett's imagination was sparked by the possibility of free-floating planets existing without suns. He learned later that such worlds do indeed exist and are difficult to detect due to their darkness. Astronomers have used gravitational lensing to identify several examples of these planets, which are thought to be capable of supporting life. The author didn't aim to create a scientifically accurate world when writing Dark Eden. Instead, he focused on developing a coherent narrative that would guide his imagination and make the story believable. Beckett's goal was not to educate readers about planetary science but to craft an engaging tale told from the perspective of its characters. Beckett didn't conduct extensive research on the topic before writing the novel. His aim was to create a sense of authenticity in the world he had created, rather than provide scientific explanations for its workings. The story is presented through the eyes of its inhabitants, who are unaware of the underlying principles governing their environment. The idea of life thriving on a sunless planet has sparked debate among scientists and science fiction enthusiasts alike. While Beckett's vision may differ from current understanding, it highlights the possibility that life can exist in unexpected environments. The concept raises intriguing questions about the conditions necessary for life to emerge and sustain itself in the universe. The idea was to create a habitable environment on Eden by utilizing its internal heat sources. This concept led me to propose that the planet's hot core would have allowed for liquid water to exist beneath a thick layer of ice. The presence of liquid water is essential for life as we know it, and I hypothesized that this condition could have given rise to life forms adapted to the unique conditions on Eden. One of these life forms was a peculiar organism resembling tree roots. It had evolved to tap into the heat emanating from the planet's hot rocks, using its sap-like fluid to warm the rocks and then pumping it back up to the surface. This process allowed the organism to harness energy from the geothermal activity beneath Eden's icy crust. As these organisms continued to thrive, they began to exert a profound influence on their environment. By pushing upwards into the ice shell, they melted sections of it, releasing trapped nutrients that were then absorbed by the organisms themselves. This process had a cumulative effect, ultimately resulting in the creation of habitable surface areas and an atmosphere capable of supporting human life. The thawing of Eden's surface laid the groundwork for the emergence of diverse ecosystems. Over millions of years, these ecosystems evolved into complex systems teeming with life forms that were adapted to the planet's unique conditions. This process paved the way for my subsequent stories set on Eden, where a community of humans struggled to eke out a living in this alien environment. The human settlement on Eden was characterized by a primitive technology based on stone and wood tools. The inhabitants of this isolated world lived in awe of their ancestors' stories about Earth, which they had heard through oral tradition. These tales spoke of a sunlit world where people could fly through the air and animals possessed mystical abilities, such as seeing into each other's minds. The cultural heritage of the Eden community was deeply rooted in these fantastical accounts from Earth. Their stories served as a reminder of their own exile from a world that was both familiar and yet utterly alien to them. As they struggled to survive on this unforgiving planet, they clung to the memories of their ancestors' experiences on the sunlit Earth, which seemed like a mythical realm in comparison to their harsh reality on Eden. The surface of Eden is home to root-like life forms that have developed into structures known as "trees by its human inhabitants. These tree-like organisms are at the center of a complex ecosystem on Eden, where other living things have evolved to rely on them for survival. One such organism is the starflower, which has adapted to live off the roots of these trees and in turn provides a vital source of Vitamin D. The absence of sunlight on Eden's surface has led to the development of bioluminescence among its life forms, with both the trees and starflowers emitting light. This eerie glow illuminates the leafless forests of Eden at night, creating an otherworldly landscape reminiscent of a moonless night on Earth. To create a believable ecosystem on Eden, I focused on designing animals that fit into a specific body plan, one that would allow them to thrive in their unique environment. This meant adopting a six-limbed pattern for large animals, which seemed like the most practical and efficient way to navigate the planet's dark landscapes. While this may seem restrictive, it's worth noting that many terrestrial animals also conform to a limited number of basic body plans - think monkeys, cows, crocodiles, and seagulls, all sharing four limbs despite their distinct differences. In contrast, Eden's six-limbed creatures have evolved in response to the planet's specific needs, with adaptations such as large eyes that can detect even the faintest glows in the dark. The evolution of bioluminescence on Eden has also led to some fascinating changes in the way plants and animals interact - for example, trees use luminous lanternflowers to attract pollinators, just like terrestrial flowers rely on color and scent. These imaginative creatures are not just aesthetically pleasing, but also serve as a thought-provoking exercise in what life might be like on a world without sunlight. The limitations of a sunless world are starkly apparent in Eden's ecosystem, where even the most ingenious attempts at simulating sunlight fall short of sustaining liquid water or a warm atmosphere. When crafting fictional worlds like Eden, science is often adapted and modified to suit the narrative, rather than adhering strictly to scientific principles. This approach allows for creative freedom and can lead to innovative solutions that might not be feasible in reality. The use of fiction science" is a common practice in science fiction writing, where authors take liberties with established knowledge to advance their stories. Dark Eden is no exception, as I drew upon various scientific concepts while also incorporating elements of poetic license. In addition to the planet's unique environment, the backstory of how humans arrived on Eden is also shrouded in mystery. The convenience of faster-than-light travel allows for a more streamlined narrative, although this aspect is likely to be at odds with current scientific understanding. The dark and foreboding atmosphere of Eden serves as a poignant reminder that its inhabitants are exiles, forever separated from their ancestral homeworld. This sense of loss and longing is woven throughout the story, which explores themes of exile and redemption. The symbolism of the circle of stones, marking the site where human ancestors first landed on Eden, represents the fragile hope of return and redemption that sustains the community. The project I was involved in, initiated by Comma Press, brought together writers and astronomers from Jodrell Bank to create an anthology called Firmament. Each writer collaborated with an astronomer to craft a unique story based on their shared expertise. My partner, Ida Janiak, helped me develop a scenario for a free-floating planet called Lupus, which is similar in size to Earth but has distinct characteristics. Unlike the hypothetical planet Eden, Lupus's surface is covered by a thick layer of ice that won't melt, with a liquid ocean beneath it. The story we created imagines life on Lupus, a planet that shares some similarities with Europa, a moon of Jupiter.
